title: Barbershops: The Last Third Place
author: Nick Sledge
summary: Nick Sledge opens with his lifelong loyalty to a single barbershop (since age four, alongside his father) as a model of an institution worth keeping. He traces barbershop history from Roman tonsores through medieval barber-surgeons to colonial America, where the shop functioned as a hub for news and civic argument. Drawing on sociologist Ray Oldenburg's concept of the 'third place,' he argues the barbershop is nearly the last surviving example as pubs, diners, and town squares have disappeared, and that the loss of such places has produced loneliness and polarization. He distinguishes a trained barber from a stylist, frames grooming as a matter of modesty rather than vanity, and closes arguing that presentation is a form of respect.
points: Applies Ray Oldenburg's 'third place' sociology directly to the barbershop, arguing it's nearly the last one left.
Traces a long institutional history to argue the barbershop's social function predates and outlasts fashion trends.
Frames grooming as modesty rather than vanity, with a theological grounding rather than pure self-improvement rhetoric.
Closes with concrete, usable guidance — presentation as a form of respect — making the essay practical, not just nostalgic.
quotes: That barbershop was Fern Creek Barber Shop in Louisville KY. I have been going ever since.
In the American colonies, the barbershop was where news moved through the town, where civic arguments were made and where men showed up and acted like somebody.
The barbershop is a shining example of a Third Place and in modern times, while a bit tougher to find, it seems to be one of the last.
The loss of more and more third places created lonelier people and ultimately a more polarized society.
A barber is not a stylist. This matters. A barber is a licensed and trained professional for men's hair.
How a man presents himself is plenty of communication and sometimes the only chance you get at it.
If there is anything that I wish for someone to take from this article over anything else is that presentation is a form of respect. That includes a haircut.
